newsitem.title: UK: Foreigners stampede for stock in Russia's Gazprom.
newsitem.headline: Foreigners stampede for stock in Russia's Gazprom.

text.p: Foreign investors shrugged off turmoil in the Kremlin in their clamour for stock in Russia's RAO Gazprom, the world's largest natural gas supplier.
On Tuesday, the company said that its American Depositary Share (ADS) offering, Russia's largest overseas share issue, had raised $373.3 million at a price of $15.75 per ADS.
"We are delighted by the strong interest in the global offering and in the significant level of oversubscription," said Rem Vyakhirev, chairman of Gazprom's management committee.

The issue was around five times oversubscribed, following a turbulent week of dark talk of rebellion in Russia culminating in the sacking by President Boris Yeltsin of his national security adviser, Alexander Lebed.
Pricing for the ADS had been indicated at $14.00-$16.00 and each ADS is equivalent to 10 underlying shares.
If an over-allotment option of 15 percent of the issue is exercised, Gazprom could raise up to $429.3 million.
That equals total foreign investment in the whole of the Russian stock market and values Gazprom at $37 billion, against $21 billion for the RTS-24 index of leading Russian shares.
But investors say Gazprom's numbers made it compelling.
It supplies 21 percent of the natural gas consumed in western Europe and controls 94 percent of Russian natural gas production and 23 percent of global production.
Reserves of 32 trillion cubic metres of natural gas are 24 times those of Royal Dutch Shell and 28 times those of Exxon.
The ADS comes as part of Gazprom's attempt sell a total of nine percent of its stock overseas and to win a listing in New York once it has completed its accounts U.S. standards.
An overseas offer had been mulled in 1994, but collapsed in the wake of the Mexican financial crisis of that year and wrangles over the value of Gazprom.
"The global offering is an important step in Gazprom's establishment in the capital markets as the leading pan-European energy company," Vyakhirev said.
If the over-allotment option is exercised, nearly two percent of Gazprom's stock will be in foreign hands.

Investors paid more than three times the 48 cents they would pay for shares in Moscow, as the ADS offers a dollar-denominated, euro-clearable security which avoids the difficulty of direct rouble exposure and dealing on Russian stock exchanges as well tight control of the underlying shares by Gazprom.
They were keen to buy despite the political uncertainty generated by Yeltsin's heart operation and the regulatory and tax framework for Gazprom.
During the two week offer period for the shares, the Russian government said it had frozen the assets of the company's main operating subsidiary.

The fact that so much foreign money had been earmarked for one Russian company, albeit the bluest of blue chips and one with connections at the highest level of government -- Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin used to run the company -- is encouraging ahead of the country's entry to the International Finance Corp and Morgan Stanley share indexes.
"This could presage a huge flow of foreign money in to Russia. After all that has happened with Gazprom's assets being frozen and the political turmoil," said one fund manager.

The company has a $40 billion expansion plan over the next 10 years to develop new gas fields as well as a a 5,900 kilometre pipeline from Western Siberia to Germany which will help boost exports from 117.4 billion cubic metres of gas to Western Europe in 1995 to 154 billion cubic metres by the end of 1998 and more once the pipeline is completed.
